intro.text:
Air flows along a channel and over a sudden step down.

What happens in the corner behind the step?

captions.text: The air is switched on at 7.65 m/s. The grey block is a 1 cm step; colours show where the air spins.
The flow cannot turn the sharp corner. It breaks away, and a starting vortex rolls up behind the step.
The vortex grows until it is swept downstream, and the next one starts at once.
From now on a new vortex leaves the step every 23 ms: 44 vortices per second.
Each vortex drags fluid with it. Next to the floor, under the vortices, the air flows backwards towards the step.
Averaged over time, this backflow forms a bubble 3.5 step heights long.

outro.text:
One vortex every 23 ms, a backflow bubble 3.5 steps long.
In real 3D turbulence the vortices break up and the bubble is 6.3 steps long: 2D vortices stay too strong.

OpenFOAM pimpleFoam · 2D LES, Re = 5100

reels.name: dye
reels.bar_title: Dye released near the floor of the inlet

captions.text: Dye marks the slow air near the floor of the inlet channel. The grey block is a 1 cm step.
At the corner the dye is lifted off the wall and wound into a spiral: the starting vortex.
The spiral is swept away, and the next vortex starts rolling up more dye.
Some dye is pulled backwards into the corner behind the step and stays there.
This stirring costs energy: it is why separated flow adds drag behind cars and losses in pipes and diffusers.

outro.text:
The shear layer behind the step rolls up into a vortex every 23 ms and stirs the dye into the corner.

OpenFOAM pimpleFoam · 2D LES, Re = 5100
